From our help article "Multi-factor authentication setup and recovery":
- Ask the user to check that automatic time synchronisation is enabled on the device generating the code. Drift is the most common cause by a wide margin.
- If the device is lost, the user should sign in with one of their recovery codes and then re-enrol a new device from the security page.
- Where no recovery codes are available, an account administrator can reset multi-factor authentication for that user from the team members page.
- If the user is the sole administrator and has no recovery codes, identity verification through support is required and takes up to one business day.
- Support cannot disable multi-factor authentication without identity verification, regardless of urgency.
Common causes listed in the article:
- Device clock drift of more than thirty seconds invalidates time-based codes
- The authenticator was enrolled against a different account
- Recovery codes were regenerated, invalidating the older set

Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Pagination and handling large result sets":
- Use cursor pagination for anything that may change while you iterate. Offset pagination will skip or repeat records when items are inserted mid-iteration.
- Pass the next_cursor value from each response as the cursor parameter of the following request, and stop when it is null.
- Keep page size at or below two hundred. Larger requests are rejected rather than truncated.
- For very large extracts, use the export endpoint, which runs asynchronously and returns a download link.
- Cursors expire after one hour.
- Long-running iterations should handle expiry by restarting from a recorded checkpoint.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The cursor from the previous response was not passed to the next request
- Offset pagination was used against a changing collection
- The page size requested exceeds the maximum

From our help article "Container deployments failing during the health check phase":
- Confirm the container is listening on the port declared in the service definition. A mismatch here produces a health check failure that looks like a timeout.
- Increase the initial delay if the application needs time to warm up before it can answer. Thirty seconds is a reasonable starting point for services that load models or caches.
- Compare the environment variables present in the deployment against those the application requires. Missing configuration frequently causes a silent startup failure.
- Inspect the container logs from the failed revision rather than the running one; the rollback replaces the logs shown by default.
- A health check must return within the timeout using only local state.
- Endpoints that call a database will fail during a database incident and take the service down with them.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The health endpoint takes longer to respond than the configured timeout
- The container listens on a different port than the service declares
- A required environment variable is absent in the deployed environment

From our help article "Database connection pool exhaustion":
- Calculate the total possible connections as pool size multiplied by maximum instances, and compare it against your plan's connection limit.

- Consider a connection proxy if the instance count must remain high, so that pooling happens once rather than per instance.
- The connection limit is a property of the database plan and is listed on the plan comparison page.

- Connections are not being returned to the pool after use

Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Configuring environment variables and secrets":
- Check the scope at which the variable was defined. Service scope overrides project scope, and project scope overrides organisation defaults.
- Store anything sensitive as a secret rather than a variable. Secrets are masked in logs and are not readable through the API after creation.
- Review the environment overrides page, which lists values that differ from the defaults for each environment.
- Redeploy after changing configuration. Running containers do not pick up new values without a restart.
- A secret that has been printed to logs should be treated as exposed and rotated, even if the logs are private.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The variable was set at project scope but read at service scope
- The application logs its configuration at startup
- An environment override exists that is not visible on the main settings page

results.sent_text:
Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Diagnosing elevated response latency":
- Compare median and 95th percentile latency on the metrics page. A large gap points to contention or queueing rather than a uniformly slower service.
- Check memory utilisation across instances. Sustained utilisation above eighty per cent typically shows up as latency before it shows up as failure.
- Review the dependency timing breakdown on the trace view to identify whether the time is being spent in your service or waiting on another.
- Adjust the autoscaling policy if load is predictable. Scaling on request count responds sooner than scaling on processor utilisation.
- Cold starts affect the first request to a new instance.
- Frequent scaling events will therefore raise the 95th percentile even when the service itself is healthy.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The service is running close to its memory limit and spending time in garbage collection
- A downstream dependency has slowed and the delay is propagating
- Instance count is not scaling with the load pattern

- Check the current period usage against the plan allowance on the billing page.

- A spend cap was configured and reached

Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Resolving invalid credential errors on login":
- Confirm whether the account is locked by checking the security page of the console. A locked account displays a red banner and unlocks automatically after thirty minutes.
- Clear cookies for the CloudServe domain, or open a private browsing window, then attempt the login again.
- If the CLI is failing, run `cloudserve auth logout` followed by `cloudserve auth login` to discard the cached token.
- Where the account remains locked and the customer needs immediate access, an administrator on the account can release the lock from the team members page.
- Repeated lockouts within a short period usually indicate an automated process still using an old password rather than a user error.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The account is locked after five consecutive failed attempts
- A stale session cookie is being sent alongside new credentials
- The password was changed in another session and the client cached the old one

Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Diagnosing elevated response latency":
- Compare median and 95th percentile latency on the metrics page. A large gap points to contention or queueing rather than a uniformly slower service.
- Check memory utilisation across instances. Sustained utilisation above eighty per cent typically shows up as latency before it shows up as failure.
- Review the dependency timing breakdown on the trace view to identify whether the time is being spent in your service or waiting on another.
- Adjust the autoscaling policy if load is predictable. Scaling on request count responds sooner than scaling on processor utilisation.
- Cold starts affect the first request to a new instance.
- Frequent scaling events will therefore raise the 95th percentile even when the service itself is healthy.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The service is running close to its memory limit and spending time in garbage collection
- A downstream dependency has slowed and the delay is propagating
- Instance count is not scaling with the load pattern

- A spend cap was configured and reached
- Overage protection is disabled, so usage continued beyond the allowance

Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Understanding API rate limits and quota tiers":
- Read the rate limit headers returned with every response. They give the limit, the remaining allowance and the reset time, which is more reliable than inferring the limit from behaviour.
- Confirm whether the endpoint has a specific limit. Search and export endpoints are more expensive and are limited more tightly than reads.
- Implement exponential backoff with jitter on 429 responses rather than retrying immediately, which prolongs the throttling.
- Where sustained higher throughput is genuinely required, the limit can be raised on Business and Enterprise plans through an account request.
- Limits are enforced per organisation.
- Issuing more keys does not increase the available quota.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The limit applies per organisation rather than per key
- Burst capacity was consumed and the sustained rate now applies
- The endpoint being called has a lower limit than the general one

From our help article "Configuring environment variables and secrets":
- Check the scope at which the variable was defined. Service scope overrides project scope, and project scope overrides organisation defaults.
- Store anything sensitive as a secret rather than a variable. Secrets are masked in logs and are not readable through the API after creation.

- A secret that has been printed to logs should be treated as exposed and rotated, even if the logs are private.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The variable was set at project scope but read at service scope
- The application logs its configuration at startup
- An environment override exists that is not visible on the main settings page

Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Webhook delivery, retries and signature verification":
- Check the webhook delivery log, which records every attempt with the response status and body for the last seven days.
- Return 2xx as quickly as possible and process the event asynchronously. Deliveries time out after five seconds.
- Compute the signature over the raw request body before any parsing. Re-serialising JSON changes the bytes and invalidates the signature.
- Make your handler idempotent using the event identifier. At-least-once delivery means duplicates are expected rather than exceptional.
- Failed deliveries are retried with backoff for twenty-four hours, after which the endpoint is disabled and the account is notified.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The endpoint returned a non-2xx status and delivery is being retried
- The endpoint responded too slowly and the delivery timed out
- The signature was computed over a parsed body rather than the raw bytes

From our help article "Container deployments failing during the health check phase":
- Confirm the container is listening on the port declared in the service definition. A mismatch here produces a health check failure that looks like a timeout.
- Increase the initial delay if the application needs time to warm up before it can answer. Thirty seconds is a reasonable starting point for services that load models or caches.

- Inspect the container logs from the failed revision rather than the running one; the rollback replaces the logs shown by default.
- A health check must return within the timeout using only local state.
- Endpoints that call a database will fail during a database incident and take the service down with them.

- The health endpoint takes longer to respond than the configured timeout
- The container listens on a different port than the service declares
- A required environment variable is absent in the deployed environment

results.sent_text:
Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Database connection pool exhaustion":
- Calculate the total possible connections as pool size multiplied by maximum instances, and compare it against your plan's connection limit.
- Reduce the per-instance pool size rather than raising the limit. A large number of small pools is usually the wrong shape for a scaled service.

Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Database connection pool exhaustion":
- Calculate the total possible connections as pool size multiplied by maximum instances, and compare it against your plan's connection limit.
- Reduce the per-instance pool size rather than raising the limit. A large number of small pools is usually the wrong shape for a scaled service.
- Look for queries that hold a transaction open across a network call to another service, which is the most common cause of leaks of this kind.
- Consider a connection proxy if the instance count must remain high, so that pooling happens once rather than per instance.
- The connection limit is a property of the database plan and is listed on the plan comparison page.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The pool size multiplied by the instance count exceeds the database connection limit
- Connections are not being returned to the pool after use
- Long-running transactions are holding connections open

From our help article "Single sign-on configuration with SAML providers":
- Compare the assertion consumer service URL in your identity provider against the value shown on the SSO settings page. They must match exactly, including the trailing path.

- SAML changes take effect immediately for new sessions but existing sessions remain valid until they expire.

- The assertion consumer service URL does not match the value registered with CloudServe
- The email attribute in the assertion does not match the CloudServe account email

From our help article "API key rotation and scope management":
- Check the API keys page for the key's status and expiry. Revoked and expired keys are listed with the date and the user who acted.
- Review the scopes attached to the key. Read-only keys cannot write, and project-scoped keys cannot reach organisation endpoints.
- To rotate without downtime, create the replacement key first, deploy it, confirm traffic has moved, then revoke the old key.
- If a key has been exposed publicly, revoke it immediately rather than waiting for the rotation window.
- Keys issued to individual users are removed when that user is deleted.
- Use service accounts for anything running in production.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The key was revoked or reached its configured expiry
- The key was issued with a scope that excludes the endpoint being called
- The key belongs to a deleted user and was removed with the account

**Applies to:** Container Service

## Symptoms

- The deployment reaches running and then rolls back
- Logs show repeated health check timeouts
- The service works locally but not when deployed

## Common causes
sentences: 1. Confirm the container is listening on the port declared in the service definition.
1. A mismatch here produces a health check failure that looks like a timeout.

2. Thirty seconds is a reasonable starting point for services that load models or caches.
3. Compare the environment variables present in the deployment against those the application requires.
3. Missing configuration frequently causes a silent startup failure.
4. Inspect the container logs from the failed revision rather than the running one; the rollback replaces the logs shown by default.
5. A health check must return within the timeout using only local state.
6. Endpoints that call a database will fail during a database incident and take the service down with them.
7. The health endpoint takes longer to respond than the configured timeout.
8. The container listens on a different port than the service declares.
9. A required environment variable is absent in the deployed environment.

From our help article "Diagnosing elevated response latency":
- Compare median and 95th percentile latency on the metrics page. A large gap points to contention or queueing rather than a uniformly slower service.

- Frequent scaling events will therefore raise the 95th percentile even when the service itself is healthy.

- Check the API keys page for the key's status and expiry. Revoked and expired keys are listed with the date and the user who acted.
- Review the scopes attached to the key. Read-only keys cannot write, and project-scoped keys cannot reach organisation endpoints.
- To rotate without downtime, create the replacement key first, deploy it, confirm traffic has moved, then revoke the old key.
- If a key has been exposed publicly, revoke it immediately rather than waiting for the rotation window.

## Symptoms

- Response times have increased without a code change
- The 95th percentile is far above the median
- Latency rises at predictable times of day

## Common causes
sentences: 1. Compare median and 95th percentile latency on the metrics page.
1. A large gap points to contention or queueing rather than a uniformly slower service.
2. Check memory utilisation across instances.
2. Sustained utilisation above eighty per cent typically shows up as latency before it shows up as failure.
3. Review the dependency timing breakdown on the trace view to identify whether the time is being spent in your service or waiting on another.
4. Adjust the autoscaling policy if load is predictable.
4. Scaling on request count responds sooner than scaling on processor utilisation.
5. Cold starts affect the first request to a new instance.
6. Frequent scaling events will therefore raise the 95th percentile even when the service itself is healthy.
7. The service is running close to its memory limit and spending time in garbage collection.
8. A downstream dependency has slowed and the delay is propagating.
9. Instance count is not scaling with the load pattern.

Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Container deployments failing during the health check phase":
- Confirm the container is listening on the port declared in the service definition. A mismatch here produces a health check failure that looks like a timeout.
- Increase the initial delay if the application needs time to warm up before it can answer. Thirty seconds is a reasonable starting point for services that load models or caches.
- Compare the environment variables present in the deployment against those the application requires. Missing configuration frequently causes a silent startup failure.
- Inspect the container logs from the failed revision rather than the running one; the rollback replaces the logs shown by default.
- A health check must return within the timeout using only local state.
- Endpoints that call a database will fail during a database incident and take the service down with them.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The health endpoint takes longer to respond than the configured timeout
- The container listens on a different port than the service declares
- A required environment variable is absent in the deployed environment

results.sent_text:
Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Webhook delivery, retries and signature verification":
- Check the webhook delivery log, which records every attempt with the response status and body for the last seven days.
- Return 2xx as quickly as possible and process the event asynchronously. Deliveries time out after five seconds.
- Compute the signature over the raw request body before any parsing. Re-serialising JSON changes the bytes and invalidates the signature.
- Make your handler idempotent using the event identifier. At-least-once delivery means duplicates are expected rather than exceptional.
- Failed deliveries are retried with backoff for twenty-four hours, after which the endpoint is disabled and the account is notified.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The endpoint returned a non-2xx status and delivery is being retried
- The endpoint responded too slowly and the delivery timed out
- The signature was computed over a parsed body rather than the raw bytes

Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Diagnosing elevated response latency":
- Compare median and 95th percentile latency on the metrics page. A large gap points to contention or queueing rather than a uniformly slower service.
- Check memory utilisation across instances. Sustained utilisation above eighty per cent typically shows up as latency before it shows up as failure.
- Review the dependency timing breakdown on the trace view to identify whether the time is being spent in your service or waiting on another.
- Adjust the autoscaling policy if load is predictable. Scaling on request count responds sooner than scaling on processor utilisation.
- Cold starts affect the first request to a new instance.
- Frequent scaling events will therefore raise the 95th percentile even when the service itself is healthy.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The service is running close to its memory limit and spending time in garbage collection
- A downstream dependency has slowed and the delay is propagating
- Instance count is not scaling with the load pattern

# Diagnosing elevated response latency

**Applies to:** All compute services

## Symptoms

- Response times have increased without a code change
- The 95th percentile is far above the median
- Latency rises at predictable times of day

## Common causes
sentences: 1. Compare median and 95th percentile latency on the metrics page.
1. A large gap points to contention or queueing rather than a uniformly slower service.
2. Check memory utilisation across instances.
2. Sustained utilisation above eighty per cent typically shows up as latency before it shows up as failure.
3. Review the dependency timing breakdown on the trace view to identify whether the time is being spent in your service or waiting on another.
4. Adjust the autoscaling policy if load is predictable.
4. Scaling on request count responds sooner than scaling on processor utilisation.
5. Cold starts affect the first request to a new instance.
6. Frequent scaling events will therefore raise the 95th percentile even when the service itself is healthy.
7. The service is running close to its memory limit and spending time in garbage collection.
8. A downstream dependency has slowed and the delay is propagating.
9. Instance count is not scaling with the load pattern.

Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Webhook delivery, retries and signature verification":
- Check the webhook delivery log, which records every attempt with the response status and body for the last seven days.
- Return 2xx as quickly as possible and process the event asynchronously. Deliveries time out after five seconds.
- Compute the signature over the raw request body before any parsing. Re-serialising JSON changes the bytes and invalidates the signature.
- Make your handler idempotent using the event identifier. At-least-once delivery means duplicates are expected rather than exceptional.
- Failed deliveries are retried with backoff for twenty-four hours, after which the endpoint is disabled and the account is notified.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The endpoint returned a non-2xx status and delivery is being retried
- The endpoint responded too slowly and the delivery timed out
- The signature was computed over a parsed body rather than the raw bytes

From our help article "Migrating an existing application to CloudServe":
- Externalise configuration before migrating. Anything read from a file on disk should move to environment variables or secrets.
- Identify local state such as uploaded files or session data and move it to object storage or the managed database first.
- Run in parallel with the existing deployment and shift a small share of traffic before committing to the move.
- Plan the database migration separately from the application migration; attempting both at once makes any failure hard to diagnose.
- Applications that write to the local filesystem will lose that data on every deployment and every scaling event.
Common causes listed in the article:
- Configuration is embedded in the application rather than externalised
- The application depends on local state that will not survive scaling

From our help article "Database connection pool exhaustion":
- Calculate the total possible connections as pool size multiplied by maximum instances, and compare it against your plan's connection limit.

- The pool size multiplied by the instance count exceeds the database connection limit
- Connections are not being returned to the pool after use

results.sent_text:
Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Backups, retention and point-in-time restore":
- Identify the point you need to restore to. Point-in-time recovery covers any moment within the retention window rather than only backup times.
- Restore into a new database instance rather than over the existing one, so the current state is preserved while you verify the restore.
- Allow roughly ten minutes per hundred gigabytes for the restore, and considerably longer where the instance is also under load.
- Verify the restored data before switching traffic, and keep the original instance until that verification is complete.
- Retention is seven days on Standard, thirty days on Business and ninety days on Enterprise plans.
Common causes listed in the article:
- Automated backups run daily and retention depends on the plan
- Restore time scales with database size
- Point-in-time recovery is available only where continuous archiving is enabled

From our help article "Database connection pool exhaustion":
- Calculate the total possible connections as pool size multiplied by maximum instances, and compare it against your plan's connection limit.
- Reduce the per-instance pool size rather than raising the limit. A large number of small pools is usually the wrong shape for a scaled service.
- Look for queries that hold a transaction open across a network call to another service, which is the most common cause of leaks of this kind.
- Consider a connection proxy if the instance count must remain high, so that pooling happens once rather than per instance.

# Pagination and handling large result sets

**Applies to:** All plans

## Symptoms

- Only the first page of results is returned
- Iterating through results misses or duplicates records
- Large queries time out

## Common causes
sentences: 1. Use cursor pagination for anything that may change while you iterate.
1. Offset pagination will skip or repeat records when items are inserted mid-iteration.
2. Pass the next_cursor value from each response as the cursor parameter of the following request, and stop when it is null.
3. Keep page size at or below two hundred.
3. Larger requests are rejected rather than truncated.
4. For very large extracts, use the export endpoint, which runs asynchronously and returns a download link.
5. Cursors expire after one hour.
6. Long-running iterations should handle expiry by restarting from a recorded checkpoint.
7. The cursor from the previous response was not passed to the next request.
8. Offset pagination was used against a changing collection.
9. The page size requested exceeds the maximum.

Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Understanding API rate limits and quota tiers":
- Read the rate limit headers returned with every response. They give the limit, the remaining allowance and the reset time, which is more reliable than inferring the limit from behaviour.
- Confirm whether the endpoint has a specific limit. Search and export endpoints are more expensive and are limited more tightly than reads.
- Implement exponential backoff with jitter on 429 responses rather than retrying immediately, which prolongs the throttling.
- Where sustained higher throughput is genuinely required, the limit can be raised on Business and Enterprise plans through an account request.
- Limits are enforced per organisation.
- Issuing more keys does not increase the available quota.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The limit applies per organisation rather than per key
- Burst capacity was consumed and the sustained rate now applies
- The endpoint being called has a lower limit than the general one

Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Diagnosing elevated response latency":
- Compare median and 95th percentile latency on the metrics page. A large gap points to contention or queueing rather than a uniformly slower service.
- Check memory utilisation across instances. Sustained utilisation above eighty per cent typically shows up as latency before it shows up as failure.
- Review the dependency timing breakdown on the trace view to identify whether the time is being spent in your service or waiting on another.
- Adjust the autoscaling policy if load is predictable. Scaling on request count responds sooner than scaling on processor utilisation.
- Cold starts affect the first request to a new instance.
- Frequent scaling events will therefore raise the 95th percentile even when the service itself is healthy.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The service is running close to its memory limit and spending time in garbage collection
- A downstream dependency has slowed and the delay is propagating
- Instance count is not scaling with the load pattern

Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Webhook delivery, retries and signature verification":
- Check the webhook delivery log, which records every attempt with the response status and body for the last seven days.
- Return 2xx as quickly as possible and process the event asynchronously. Deliveries time out after five seconds.
- Compute the signature over the raw request body before any parsing. Re-serialising JSON changes the bytes and invalidates the signature.
- Make your handler idempotent using the event identifier. At-least-once delivery means duplicates are expected rather than exceptional.
- Failed deliveries are retried with backoff for twenty-four hours, after which the endpoint is disabled and the account is notified.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The endpoint returned a non-2xx status and delivery is being retried
- The endpoint responded too slowly and the delivery timed out
- The signature was computed over a parsed body rather than the raw bytes

Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Multi-factor authentication setup and recovery":
- Ask the user to check that automatic time synchronisation is enabled on the device generating the code. Drift is the most common cause by a wide margin.
- If the device is lost, the user should sign in with one of their recovery codes and then re-enrol a new device from the security page.
- Where no recovery codes are available, an account administrator can reset multi-factor authentication for that user from the team members page.
- If the user is the sole administrator and has no recovery codes, identity verification through support is required and takes up to one business day.
- Support cannot disable multi-factor authentication without identity verification, regardless of urgency.
Common causes listed in the article:
- Device clock drift of more than thirty seconds invalidates time-based codes
- The authenticator was enrolled against a different account
- Recovery codes were regenerated, invalidating the older set

Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Usage limits, overage and spend controls":
- Check the current period usage against the plan allowance on the billing page.
- Decide deliberately between a hard spend cap, which stops the service, and overage, which continues at the listed rate. Production workloads generally need the second.
- Configure alerts at fifty, eighty and ninety-five per cent of allowance rather than relying on the cap as a warning.
- Where a cap has stopped a production service, an account owner can raise it immediately from the billing page and service resumes within a minute.
- Spend caps apply per organisation and cannot currently be set per project.
Common causes listed in the article:
- Plan allowance was consumed before the end of the period
- A spend cap was configured and reached
- Overage protection is disabled, so usage continued beyond the allowance

Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Build failures caused by dependency resolution":
- Pin your dependencies with exact versions and commit the lock file. Unpinned dependencies are the cause in the large majority of cases of this kind.
- Compare the runtime version declared in your build configuration against the version you use locally.
- Clear the build cache from the settings page and trigger a fresh build to rule out a corrupted artefact.
- If a specific dependency is failing to resolve, check whether its registry is reachable from the build network.
- Build logs retain the full resolution output for thirty days, which is usually enough to identify which version changed.
Common causes listed in the article:
- An unpinned dependency released a new incompatible version
- The build environment uses a different language runtime than the local machine
- The dependency cache holds a partially written artefact

From our help article "Configuring environment variables and secrets":
- Check the scope at which the variable was defined. Service scope overrides project scope, and project scope overrides organisation defaults.
- Store anything sensitive as a secret rather than a variable. Secrets are masked in logs and are not readable through the API after creation.

- A secret that has been printed to logs should be treated as exposed and rotated, even if the logs are private.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The variable was set at project scope but read at service scope
- The application logs its configuration at startup
- An environment override exists that is not visible on the main settings page

results.sent_text:
Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Webhook delivery, retries and signature verification":
- Check the webhook delivery log, which records every attempt with the response status and body for the last seven days.
- Return 2xx as quickly as possible and process the event asynchronously. Deliveries time out after five seconds.
- Compute the signature over the raw request body before any parsing. Re-serialising JSON changes the bytes and invalidates the signature.
- Make your handler idempotent using the event identifier. At-least-once delivery means duplicates are expected rather than exceptional.
- Failed deliveries are retried with backoff for twenty-four hours, after which the endpoint is disabled and the account is notified.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The endpoint returned a non-2xx status and delivery is being retried
- The endpoint responded too slowly and the delivery timed out
- The signature was computed over a parsed body rather than the raw bytes

Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Understanding API rate limits and quota tiers":
- Read the rate limit headers returned with every response. They give the limit, the remaining allowance and the reset time, which is more reliable than inferring the limit from behaviour.
- Confirm whether the endpoint has a specific limit. Search and export endpoints are more expensive and are limited more tightly than reads.
- Implement exponential backoff with jitter on 429 responses rather than retrying immediately, which prolongs the throttling.

- Limits are enforced per organisation.
- Issuing more keys does not increase the available quota.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The limit applies per organisation rather than per key
- Burst capacity was consumed and the sustained rate now applies
- The endpoint being called has a lower limit than the general one

From our help article "Database connection pool exhaustion":
- Calculate the total possible connections as pool size multiplied by maximum instances, and compare it against your plan's connection limit.

- The pool size multiplied by the instance count exceeds the database connection limit
- Connections are not being returned to the pool after use
- Long-running transactions are holding connections open

Thanks for getting in touch. Here is what to do:

From our help article "Diagnosing elevated response latency":
- Compare median and 95th percentile latency on the metrics page. A large gap points to contention or queueing rather than a uniformly slower service.
- Check memory utilisation across instances. Sustained utilisation above eighty per cent typically shows up as latency before it shows up as failure.
- Review the dependency timing breakdown on the trace view to identify whether the time is being spent in your service or waiting on another.
- Adjust the autoscaling policy if load is predictable. Scaling on request count responds sooner than scaling on processor utilisation.
- Cold starts affect the first request to a new instance.
- Frequent scaling events will therefore raise the 95th percentile even when the service itself is healthy.
Common causes listed in the article:
- The service is running close to its memory limit and spending time in garbage collection
- A downstream dependency has slowed and the delay is propagating
- Instance count is not scaling with the load pattern

From our help article "Migrating an existing application to CloudServe":
- Externalise configuration before migrating. Anything read from a file on disk should move to environment variables or secrets.

- Applications that write to the local filesystem will lose that data on every deployment and every scaling event.

- Configuration is embedded in the application rather than externalised
- The application depends on local state that will not survive scaling
